chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): that he was asked about what the hunting spear (mi'rad) strikes of game.
He said: 'If he has no hunting arrows other than the mi'rad, and he mentions the name of Allah upon it, let him eat from what it kills; and if he has other arrows, then he should not eat.'

key_terms.الصَّيْدُ: Game or wild animals hunted for food.
key_terms.النَّبْلُ: Hunting arrows (plural of nuabl), representing other bladed hunting weapons.
key_terms.الْمِعْرَاضُ: A long, pointed hunting spear used for striking game.
key_terms.ذَكَرَ اسْمَ اللَّهِ: Mentioning the name of Allah (Tasmiyah) at the time of slaughter.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game killed by a hunting spear if the hunter has other arrows?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the mi'rad (a long, piercing spear) and other hunting tools based on the principle of 'dhabihah' suitability; if it is the sole weapon, it is treated as a valid slaughter instrument provided Allah's name is invoked. However, if the hunter possesses other arrows or blades, the mi'rad is deemed insufficient for proper slaughter due to its piercing nature rather than cutting, rendering the game non-permissible. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the method of death (bleeding out) in determining the ritual purity of wild game.
